title: The Democrats Who Voted Against Nominating Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker of the House
author: Chantelle Lee
body:
Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York secured the vast majority of House Democrats’ support in his nomination for Speaker of the House. Eleven members of his party, however, voted against giving him the nod.

The ballots were cast in secret, so the identities of some of the Democrats who cast “no” votes are not yet known. But seven progressive members-elect—Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, and Claire Valdez of New York—issued a joint statement on Wednesday, in which they revealed that they opposed Jeffries for the role.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the members-elect said in their statement. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they continued. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”

A spokesperson for Haynes released a statement on Wednesday saying that the Congressman-elect “woke up unexpectedly ill” that morning and had missed the vote, meaning that he was not among the 11 members who voted against nominating Jeffries. The spokesperson said, though, that Haynes had intended to vote no, per the joint statement.

Haynes previously spoke highly of Jeffries in an interview with TIME. “There are some people when you meet them and they’re young, you know they have the ‘it’ factor,” the member-elect said to TIME. “You know that they are hungry for knowledge. They are determined to make a difference.”

Five of the incoming lawmakers who signed onto the joint statement—Chevalier, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb, and Valdez—are Democratic socialists.

Another progressive member-elect, Don Leonard of Ohio, confirmed in a story posted on his Instagram account that he had voted against Jeffries’ nomination. Last week, Leonard shared a video on his social media account, in which he claimed that senior members of the party told him his life would become a “living hell” if he didn’t back Jeffries.

In an interview with CNN that aired on Sunday, Leonard said that he had met with Jeffries. He shared some of the issues he wanted the New York lawmaker to address, including tackling corruption and “call the question on U.S. aid to Israel.”

“What I tried to impress upon Leader Jeffries is what we need in this moment right now is not just a caucus leader, but a leader of the Democratic Party,” Leonard told CNN. “And that what I was seeing from the letter that he requested my support for his speakership was not indicative of the kind of things that my constituents need to see in order to put our faith that he is able to lead us.”

Newly-elected Angela Gonzales-Torres of California, a Democratic socialist, revealed on social media on Wednesday afternoon that she also voted “no.”

“Voters gave us a chance on November 3rd to actually make a difference in their lives. A chance to deliver on affordable housing. A chance to deliver Medicare for All. A chance to abolish ICE and hold the corrupt elite accountable,” she said. “Since day one, I have been telling leadership that Angelenos have not been satisfied with the status quo and are demanding transformative change. I voted NO today, keeping my community and the trust they instilled in me in mind.”

The other three members who voted against Jeffries’ nomination are unknown at this time.

Despite the opposition of the few holdouts, the vote on Wednesday was an overwhelming 251-11, allowing Jeffries’ nomination to sail through. No one challenged the New York lawmaker for the nomination.

The official House vote to elect the Speaker, as well as other leaders in the chamber, will take place on Jan. 3.

The backing of the House Democratic caucus, which will hold a significant majority in the next Congress, all but assures that Jeffries will win the position on the lower chamber’s floor and become the first Black American to hold the role of Speaker of the House.

When asked about his detractors during a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, Jeffries replied, “The results of today’s election speak for themselves,” adding that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.” He went on to say that it’s “an honor to be serving with a majority” in the House, with members “from all across the country” and that the party was embracing “people who have different perspectives.”

“We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people,” Jeffries said. “That’s our commitment. And the overwhelming majority of people within the caucus have spoken.”
